speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Can the minister assure the house that every avenue of investigation is being undertaken in connection with the unfortunate plane crash at Downsview airport in my constituency last Friday night?

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: INTO PLANE CRASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the most regrettable accident at Downsview is being investigated by an accident investigation team. The pilot was a qualified Tracker aircraft captain and was engaged in keeping his flying qualifications up to date. Accidents of this nature emphasize the problem of air fields near built up areas. In the case of Downsview there were over 50,000 landings and take-offs at the airfield last year, and I am informed that 55 per cent of these were by civilian aircraft. We are examining these problems very closely, and this was a subject for discussion at defence council this morning. In addition we have undertaken a review of all flying activities at Downsview.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to pay tribute to those servicemen who lost their lives in this unfortunate accident. It is a tragic loss, but we can be very thankful that others did not lose their lives.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway asked a question with reference to low grade meat supplied to the Queen Mary veterans hospital in Montreal. I now have that information. On or about December 1, I am informed, the
DEBATES	6351
Inquiries of the Ministry Queen Mary veterans hospital received a consignment of approximately 1,500 lbs. of beef bought through the Department of Defence Production from recognized meat retailers. Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
On clause 17-Powers exercisable by executive committee after consultation.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak to clause 17. I was not one of the members of the committee who asked that this clause be stood-clause 19 is the first one I asked to have stood after clause 3-and I am indebted to the committee for having stood it. The marginal note of clause 17 reads "Powers exercisable by executive committee after consultation" and subclause (1) provides as follows:
In furtherance of the objects of the council, the executive committee, after consultation with the part-time members in attendance at a meeting of the council, may
(a)	issue broadcasting licences for such terms not exceeding five years and subject to such conditions related to the circumstances of the licensee
(i) as the executive committee deems appropriate for the implementation of the broadcasting policy enunciated in section 2 of this act-
However, paragraph (b) also says:
-the executive committee, after consultation with the part-time members in attendance at a meeting of the council, may
(b)	upon application by a licensee, amend any conditions of a broadcasting licence issued to him;
I am the member for a Toronto riding, and it is only a few short months ago that quite an uproar developed in the Toronto-Barrie area over this very question of amending a licence for a broadcasting station. This involved the efforts being made by the owners of a television station in Barrie to move the station from Barrie to roughly the area of Palgrave, about 20 miles to the southwest of Barrie, which would have given them access to the Toronto market. When I say "Toronto market" I am speaking as a businessman and not as a viewer in the Toronto area of programs that are now available in that centre.
Such an uproar developed that the then minister of transport did not sign the paper which would have given them the right to move their station from Barrie to Palgrave and thus interfere with the reception of two very popular television broadcasting stations in the Niagara peninsula, in Niagara Falls and the city of Toronto.
The question I have to ask, and I am looking for a direct answer, concerns clause 17 in this new bill, which says that in furtherance of the objects of the council the executive committee, after consultation with the parttime members in attendance at a meeting of the council, may upon application by a licensee amend any conditions of a broadcasting licence issued to him. One of the conditions,
[The Chairman.]

surely, of a licence is that the licensee shall erect his broadcasting station in a certain area in order to service a certain district, because if he is not limited in his licence to the district he is going to serve he will be interfering with the electromagnetic waves that have been assigned to other broadcasters somewhat distant from him.
It is quite evident to people in the Toronto-Barrie area-and I emphasize both Barrie and Toronto-that under this clause the executive committee, after consultation with the part-time members in attendance at a meeting of the council, may upon application by a licensee amend any conditions of a broadcasting licence issued to him, without any public hearing of any kind. You may just wake up in the morning and find that the executive committee, after consultation with the part-time members in attendance at a meeting of the council, have amended a broadcasting licence upon the application of a licensee.
In Barrie there is a licensee. He has a licence to operate a broadcasting station in Barrie, with a satellite in Parry Sound and I believe a second satellite in either the village of Haliburton or the village of Minden, but in any event in the district of Haliburton.
Is there to be no public hearing on such a thing as this? It has been said that the Bourbons never remember, and they never forget. Surely to heaven this cabinet must have a little recollection of the situation that developed some months ago. It was rough enough that a sure shoo-in for a ministerial post did not get it because of the uproar that developed. Surely the Bourbons on the front benches have not forgotten that episode, or should I remind them of it?

subtopic: SUGGESTED CLOSER ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL LINKS WITH ISLANDS
SUGGESTED CLOSER ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL LINKS WITH ISLANDS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations
February 5, 1968

Trade with Caribbean Federation with the former British possessions in the West Indies which have not yet attained independence and further that, if the residents of these islands so desire it, economic and political union of these islands with the Dominion of Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not a new subject for me. I note that on June 3, 1964, June 21, 1965 and June 22, 1966, I discussed this subject matter although in somewhat different phraseology. I am now discussing it in February, 1968, and I only wish I were discussing the subject on the spot rather than here in the capital of cold Canada. The difficulties of the day have been furthered by the fact I was trying to collect my thoughts against the background of the radio coverage of the conference over in the west block.
It is, I think, appropriate that I, not as a person but as a representative of an island, continue to be interested in the subject of this resolution. We islanders have many peculiarities, some people might say, but I think we have a feeling of special kinship for these residents of the former British West Indies. I have always had a special concern with the area because in my academic years I had many students from that part of the world, and of no group of students did I have a higher opinion than of those young people. I am happy that Canadian universities have established contacts that are worth while and lasting.
The area to which I am making reference in my resolution does not, of course, cover the whole of what we used to describe as the British West Indies but rather a smaller group of islands that are not fully independent and have not followed the path of Trinidad and Tobago, Jamaica and now the Barbados. I refer to the small islands with a total population of about three quarters of a million people and a total area even smaller than the province of Prince Edward Island. I am referring to those very small islands of St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Grenada, Antigua, St. Kitts, Montserrat and Dominica. People who drink either lime juice or rum will know about some of them at least. The area is tiny but the problems are great. There is a shortage of land, a shortage of skilled labour and at the same time a tremendous overpopulation, not to mention one of the great problems, the shortage of fresh water.
In many eases these islands have a sensitive dependence upon a one-product economy, a product which often occupies a precarious position in world markets. Generally, they have a very narrow resource base. The gross

national product is low and wages are low but unemployment is high. Perhaps it is some of these latter statistics that make it possible for a maritimer in the Dominion of Canada to understand their problems. In other words, the situation of some of the people of these islands is serious as they press forward in a situation now more precarious because of political developments.
There are many problems facing our world today but one of the great problems is the disparity in the living standards of people. A hundred years ago Abraham Lincoln referred to his own country by saying, "No nation can exist half slave and half free." Can a world exist half affluent and half painfully depressed? The fractions, we know, are not precise because we know the world is not half affluent; the affluent part is a minority. I do not think the world can go on this fashion without repercussions. An enlightened people, an alert and sensitive member of the world community such as Canada is and proclaims itself to be, cannot be unaware of this sort of situation so near to us geographically.
These interesting little islands are, in a political sense, emerging nations. As political entities, of course, they are not new. In a real sense they are old communities. They have interesting traditions of British law and British institutions developed in a unique way in this unique and very beautiful part of the world. I need not, Mr. Speaker, detail the economic needs of these tiny islands. However, it is not exaggeration or condescension to say simply that both the economic and political viability of these small islands is most precarious. Sustained, massive action is required for their future stability, progress and prosperity.
The question which concerns us is, who should help and what help can be given? The United Kingdom has done much. The United States has helped. Canada has done a great deal and I am happy that the level of our assistance is rising. However, I believe that Canada is uniquely qualified to do much more in this area. Perhaps we in this area of the world could become a decisive factor in the efforts of these people for viability, both economic and political. We have close contacts with these people. Recently I read that 40 per cent of the tourist trade of the whole of what we used to call the British West Indies is made up of Canadian people. We have traded with these people over the years. Especially in the maritimes we have had close commercial contacts. We sold them our fish and
February 5, 1968

bought from them molasses and rum. I think we got the better end of the deal in terms of gustatorial satisfaction, if nothing else.
We are near to these islands. There are many parts of Canada that are closer to these islands than they are to many other parts of this dominion. Improved air service, and this I salute, is bringing us closer. In the field of transportation we are being helpful in providing improvements in air support of this area. There is much more we can do. Transportation facilities both by sea and by air can be vastly improved.
Another reason why I think we are uniquely qualified lies in our commonwealth membership. I am not yet prepared to accept the idea that the commonwealth is nothing more than a subject for effusive after-dinner speakers. I cannot but believe there is some vitality in this interesting commonwealth idea and ideal, to which Canada has given such great leadership since the days of Robert Borden.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
In this context I think there is a chance to make a vital and real contribution within the commonwealth structure. It is interesting that in the constitution of the islands to which I have referred there is a reference to them being self-governing states in free association with Great Britain, with the United Kingdom looking after their external affairs and defence. Also in their present document is the indication that the islands may change from a free state in association with Great Britain to free association with any other commonwealth countries. The process by which this change in relationship may be undertaken is a relatively simple one and can be coped with by the local government. I hope that if asked Canada would gladly and generously accept responsibility for this external aspect of sovereignty, namely, conduct of external affairs and defence. Personally, I go as far as the motion goes and say we should be willing to offer, if the peoples of these islands desire it, not only economic union but political union.
I am not unaware of the problems that might be involved here, and I will not be deluded into believing that in some of these difficult problems of race relations our country has been as Simon pure as we would sometimes seem to be when we criticize and castigate others. I am aware of all the potential problems. But surely, if three-quarters of a million people living in so small an area were to reach out for us to help them in a massive way, even to this extent, I think it would be a shame and a disgrace as well as
Trade with Caribbean Federation an indignity were we unprepared and unwilling to lend such strength as we have to assist them in their efforts toward a richer and fuller life. In any case, Mr. Speaker, if we do not reach the stage of seeing at an early day political union between Canada and the West Indies, then I hope we will do all we can this side of that development, and do all we can to aid them in the future.
I should like to close with a few words on the question of external aid to these islands. I am one of those who believe tremendously in the importance of our external aid program. When so many other aspects of diplomatic endeavours are running into great difficulty, frustration, anxiety, distress and disappointment, I still hold great hope for an enlightened external aid program.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether a country such as Canada can carry on a meaningful program of aid to 65 countries scattered all over the world. In my opinion the Canadian external aid program could be described at the present time as offering too little aid to too many. I suggest it would be the better part of wisdom to concentrate on areas where our special kind of aid could be most effective. In this area where we do a job well let us do it thoroughly as well. Let us apply ourselves to aiding those areas of the world where, with well trained personnel, full discussion with the people involved and with the full understanding that is obtained by knowledge and contact with these people, thoughtful and intelligent long-range planning and follow-through can be brought about. Let us devote our finances and energy to this end. I have no patience with those people who say: "Oh, you have troubles enough in your own country, why try to save the world?" If we wait until we solve all our own problems we will sit passive, silent and useless forever in this world of ours.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think we should establish a set of priorities, and for the reasons I have advanced this would be my first priority. I say this because of our history, our propinquity, our Commonwealth association, the indigenous need, and the opportunity for us to meet that need and perform a useful service to people facing great trials and difficulties that are inherent in their economic situation. As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Speaker, I was very happy with the meeting that took place in July, 1966, but much more needs to be done. We would delude ourselves were we to think for one moment that even with the improvements that have been made

Trade with Caribbean Federation in recent years we were measuring up not only to the demands but to our capacity to meet those demands.
There are in the maritimes some experts on the West Indies situation. One of these is Professor Fraser of Acadia University who has studied this question for many years. In an interesting report of a meeting which took place at Dalhousie University in 1966 there was a very pungent paragraph, reading as follows:
A report carried in the Financial Post of June 6, 1964, said that "Ottawa has been slightly discouraged by the snappish tone some West Indian politicians have displayed." The wonder is. of course, that there has not been more of it. West Indian leaders increasingly look to Canada for leadership and material help. It is remarkable to me that they continue to do so. It is astonishing that West Indian leaders still accept Canadian promises of concern for, and interest in, the region. Canada has over the years given the West Indians little reason to take our West Indian policy seriously. Over these years we have promised the West Indies the moon. But so far we have given them only a very little green cheese. It is not nearly enough.
Professor Fraser's remarks are a bit cryptic. Since he has uttered them we have done more. But I say again, Mr. Speaker, there is yet much more to do. I hope we will accept the challenge and move forward with all the energy we can so as to meet generously and fully the calls for aid which come from these people. If that is done I think I can say that we will have rendered on the international scene the kind of service for which we are suited, the kind of service that a country which enunciates the principles that we enunciate should render.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I personally join in this recommendation of my hon. friend from the maritimes. I think it is appropriate that he renew his plea for the West Indies because, among other reasons, of his long and proud association with Mount Allison University. Over the years Mount Allison, along with Dalhousie, Acadia, the University of New Brunswick-indeed, all the areas of higher learning where this problem is really understood-have shared basically in the thesis that has been so ably and eloquently propounded by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie). I feel that time may be running out, that while our leaders, federal and provincial, are in the confederation block discussing the unity of our own country a responsibility lies on Canada with respect to this sensitive and exotic part of the world.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
My hon. friend from Queens spoke specifically of the eastern Caribbean region, and for good reason. I believe he mentioned Montserrat, Antigua, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and St. Kitts. I also wish to refer to the West Indies area generally because I think that as Canadians we have a large and unavoidable responsibility in the entire area.
If we were more conscious of our obligations and responsibilities elsewhere perhaps our problems at home would loom less large and might be more easily and generously resolved. I know it has been contended that we must avoid establishing any constitutional arrangement with any islands which might perhaps smack of colonialism or of a colonial arrangement. The point has sometimes been made that in our relations with the West Indies we should avoid playing favourites. In
February 5, 1968

my remarks I speak for myself and not necessarily for my party. A responsible representation, I understand, will follow mine. Speaking for myself, I believe that what has been suggested in this motion is wise and sensible and in the long run will benefit Canada at home and abroad.
Does this proposal present such a great challenge, really? The hon. member has put before us two proposals, one being, in effect, union or confederation. With that I concur. If such were accomplished the benefits of our advanced economy and our expertise in many [DOT]directions would be made available to our close island friends. Is there room in our Canadian thinking and constitution for a province in the Caribbean? We should think about this seriously. The West Indian view has been ably put by H.O.B. Wooding, Q.C., who was called to the Middle Temple in 1927. He reminds us that overtures for closer Canada-West Indies trade relations were first made more than 100 years ago. At that time the West Indies were a chain of wealthy and strategic islands for the possession of which many a battle was waged. Indeed, in the history of the eighteenth century we find that the islands were regarded as more valuable than Canada. There wrere objections to economic and political movements tending to unite Canada and the islands, including the movement of free trade.
Less than 30 years later Sir John A. Macdonald appointed an adviser to himself on West Indian affairs and chose for the office Sir Francis Hincks, who had been formerly governor of Barbados. From Barbados a letter was sent by Sir Francis urging that Barbados be admitted as a member of our confederation.
The Leeward Islands also were active. Their solicitor-general, Mr. Henry Berkeley, in 1884 felt that the islands were strongly in favour of closer union with Canada. Seventy five years ago economic factors were sufficiently compelling to induce Canada and the West Indies to seek a closer relationship with each other.
I jump over to the Borden era. Professor Kenneth McNaught, in an article entitled "Should Canada 'Adopt' the West Indies", says that Francis Keefer, who was the Canadian parliamentary under secretary of state for external affairs, wrote to Borden as follows:
Now is the time, it seems to me-
Trade with Caribbean Federation
Wrote Keefer to Borden.
-for the Canadian government to quietly bring up with the Home Government the advisability of suggesting to the West Indian officials the desirability of joining the Canadian Confederation.
He went on to say:
I would dearly love to see you finish your term of office, in addition to what you have done, by adding to Confederation these British possessions in the West Atlantic.
Sir Robert Borden replied:
The question of handing over the administration of the British West Indies Island to Canada or of having them formally annexed to Canada has been under discussion with the British government more or less during the past two years.
Of course, we are not now talking about any colonial arrangement. Heaven knows, we have learned too much about the agonies that result from such arrangements. But let us go back to the nuts and bolts of such arrangements. Let us look at the hard facts, and I am referring to what Canada is selling to the West Indies. We sell flour, fish, pickled and salted, motor vehicles and parts, meats, canned fish and fabrics as well as many other commodities, but these are the half dozen most important ones. What is Canada buying from the West Indies? We buy bauxite and aluminum, sugar, crude petroleum, juices, fruit, molasses and rum. It is clear that there is a great natural advantage in a relationship between two such complementary economic areas.
Most of us are familiar with the recent representation of Hon. John Compton, chief minister of St. Lucia. May I refer to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 4, 1967. The article reads in part:
-the possibility of free trade between Canada and the Windwards was canvassed by John Compton, St. Lucia's chief minister, in Ottawa in 1965, and the idea found a warm response.
Elsewhere Sir John Compton says, "The islands are moving toward a political vacuum in the eastern Caribbean". Surely the people of North America have a great stake in freedom. This is a matter in which Canadians have an important share and a continuing concern. What is to be our contribution to an unstable world? Do we want our friends, who for many reasons cannot now look to Britain with the same confidence as before with respect to economic assistance, to feel that they are unable to rely on any real co-operation from Canada? The United States is too preoccupied to be responsive to the area's needs. Do we want these good people who
0382	COMMONS
Trade with Caribbean Federation have been brought up with a language that is common to ours, whose parliamentary traditions, culture, system of jurisprudence and system of values are common to ours-and many of those in the area who have received higher education have received it in our Canadian universities or in the United Kingdom-to feel that they must now look elsewhere for assistance, as Cuba has done?
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Sir, within the last few months we have gone through a very difficult study of our defence responsibilities and trends and we made a deliberate decision, with unification, to develop a highly mobile, elite force. Yet all the experts who talk to us about peace keeping say that such a force in 90 per cent of the occasions which can be foreseen will be used in tropical or semi-tropical conditions between 20 degrees north and 20 degrees south of the equator. How does Canada propose to train in the years ahead a highly mobile defence force? To me it is perfectly logical that we should seek, if not confederation, at least some close association with these neighbours, helping them to develop an infrastructure, helping them to improve communications, building them up, island by island, strengthening their economies and directing, as the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) suggested, far more cooperative attention to this area of the world in order that our aid might show some concrete result.
Could we not regard the British West Indies, as a great sociological workshop, where our country of 20 million people, the second richest in the world, seek to assist its friends, approximately four million people, living in a thoroughly delightful climate-the best, I am told, from the standpoint of human pleasure, in the world. Could we not so combine our affairs, so co-ordinate our enterprise and our efforts that we become, if not one country, of great comfort and assistance to each other?
If more Canadian dollars were diverted to this area-and we have been told that 40 per cent of the tourism in the West Indies is even now Canadian in origin-if we provided for our forces island training for a more effective defence posture, and if our economic assistance became adequate to this truly deserving people, then our aid could result, not in a lost cause but in a great success, simply because we had decided to use whole measures rather than half measures. I have personally every sympathy for what we are doing under the Colombo plan-I have a sister who was there
[Mr. Matheson.l
DEBATES	February 5. 1968
for some time with her husband and children. We know, too, that the Governor General and others in Canada who have had anything to do with India or Pakistan appreciate how vital this program is. And yet, as Dame Barbara Ward has said, there is a great danger of dividing and dispersing our efforts under these aid programs to such an extent that they are less than meaningful. Here is a case where by reason of history, geography and common tradition we have an unmistakable responsibility throughout the Caribbean area.
May I mention another point which is always worthy of consideration? I am turning aside from the obvious advantage of being able to find within our alliance friends whose territories complement our rigorous winter northern climate. We know that the United States has benefited very greatly from its association with St. Thomas and the Virgin Islands. Who could question the great strength which has come to the United States by the accession to the union of the wonderful state of Hawaii. We know that the French islands of Martinique and Guadeloupe have gained greater strength by their common association. I wonder whether Canada is now big enough, as Duncan Fraser and so many other scholars have suggested, to assume her proper role in this area, and to cease taking a superior attitude toward others in the world who find themselves encountering racial problems and responsibilities. Last week I spent two days in Washington wondering how it comes about that we can be so critical of our neighbours who are now trying to do big things in the realm of sociology. Are we in Canada really serious when we talk about living in a country which is strengthened by diversity? I will not easily forget the occasion on which the great Marion Anderson came down to Queen's University to get an honorary degree. Leonard Brockington helped her prepare the message she delivered, but she did it in her own inimitable way. Among other things which were memorable and moving in her words to those young people was a quotation from a poem written by an unknown Jamaican:
Dark people singing in my veins,
Fair people singing sweet strains,
And when I bow my head in prayer,
X bow with dark hands, blue eyes, red hair.
As we go through these difficult days asking ourselves how we are to make confederation in Canada more viable during the next hundred years, how we are to reconcile conflicting views on these petty differences of
February 5, 1968

language, it seems to me the suggestion put forward so eloquently by the hon. member for Queens is one which, if followed, would make us a bigger, prouder, more generous and more united people.

speechtext:
It is one
of the idiosyncracies of the Canadian parliament that on one part of our premises we should be considering-probably not too hopefully-the difficulties which are dividing us internally, while at the same time we should be considering in this chamber a suggestion that Canada has now reached a stage at which we should take over some of the duties previously performed by Britain to the extent of assisting other parts of the commonwealth through programs and policies with which we have not been associated in the past.
I have always believed we should have a close relationship with the West Indies. As a Canadian coming from a climate which even here is regarded as northerly, I can see many advantages about having available to us a winter wonderland where our people can enjoy the sunshine and the sea. Tourist revenue is nowadays a significant part of national income. I can recall figures of several years ago showing that Canada was running a trade deficit approaching $400 million on its account with the United States alone. This seems an extremely high figure having in mind the large numbers of tourists from the United States whom we see coming here each year.
The adverse balance of $400 million arises mainly because of the climatic difference between the two countries. Those who go south to the sun are accustomed to taking holidays of longer duration than do their counterparts who visit northern areas at times when our season is favourable. Then again, Americans travelling in the north are accustomed to using our national parks at low rates; they bring their own pop and other supplies to last them during a two-week stay. Canadians travelling south are not so fortunate. For obvious reasons I see a great advantage in establishing a relationship with the islands of the Caribbean which would work out to our mutual advantage.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I am often surprised at the number of things we buy from the United States-items we could just as easily buy from other countries to which we could in turn export Canadian goods. Many of the purchases we make from the United States, if we made
Trade with Caribbean Federation them from commonwealth countries with which we have close connections, could make a great difference to their balance of payments and economies. Canadian importation of bananas and citrus fruits from commonwealth countries could be significant to their economies, and yet not make so much difference to California and some of the other traditional supplying markets we have had over the years.
Such a step cannot be brought about merely by the wishes of the Canadian public. It must be by government direction and by close co-operation with these countries, after discovering what materials we have that we can exchange for goods that they can supply; and here I speak specifically of the Caribbean islands. I do not entirely agree with those who say we are now in a position to take in the Caribbean nations as part of the Canadian confederation. We do not know what the future of our confederation will be five years hence. It is quite probable that we will have something in the nature of a Suez canal running through part of Canada, and will have some difficulty servicing the maritime provinces without going through someone else's territory. Knowing this, and knowing that unless we are given more leadership than we have had in the past few years, it is foolish to talk about an economic or political union with islands far removed from the central areas of Canada. For this reason the government may not be willing to give consideration to this motion. However, trade and the exchange of tourists are matters which could be developed to the advantage of both areas.
The sponsor of the motion has discussed our role in the commonwealth, and I am in complete agreement with what he said on that topic. When I attended the recent Commonwealth Parliamentary Association meeting in Uganda I was surprised to learn how many commonwealth countries looked to Great Britain for aid when difficulties arose. It is true that Canada gives a small amount of money for such aid. I do not suggest that we can increase this amount at the moment. The reason that we cannot is that the average Canadian suffers from a lack of knowledge about external aid and its purposes.
I was also surprised to find out that aid given by the commonwealth, particularly by Great Britain, to newly developing countries was given with no strings attached. This contrasts with the American concept where you "don't give nothin' for nothin' ", where you want $2 returned for every dollar you spend,
February 5, 1968'

Trade with Caribbean Federation and you want to see that $2 now. The Americans have never given aid to any country without telling that country how much it was indebted to the United States. Yet with all the aid they have given to Korea and Viet Nam they have been unable to win many friends or accomplish much in those countries. We, living in the North American environment, will have to steer a course between the British concept of aid and the American concept.
Each time the Canadian government makes a donation to a newly developing country I get four or five letters from constituents asking, "Why in hell should we be giving money to a country we never heard of, when our old age pensions are not high enough and our other benefits are not sufficient? Why not do something for us at home before starting to give money away?" These people do not realize that the money given to other countries will bring them a return, if the proper arrangements are made. These arrangements have not been made. We have never made trade arrangements with many of the countries that we assist.
When I was in Uganda I had the opportunity, if one wishes to call it so to spend some time in a hospital. The sheets on my bed were made in England. The medicines that were supplied were made in England. The bed cover was made in Scotland. The glucose, which came in a can, was made in Ireland. In other words Britain received some benefit from the aid it provided by developing trade with Uganda.
I am sure the sponsor of this motion is not unmindful of the fact that when we may give assistance we will also expect something in return. It is not enough to supply one doctor to a newly developing country. We should be able to supply a number of doctors, establish a hospital, and thus be able to say that the Canadian people are doing something in a particular locality. No missionary sent out to the mission field can expect support without being able to show to the church sponsoring him pictures of the church he has built, the people he is helping, and the concrete results of the contributions sent to him. The average individual Canadian on the street is unable to see any results from our foreign aid.
I do not see us giving the people of the Caribbean anything more than we are likely to receive from them. But I do see more trade being developed with the entire area, including Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados and other places which were part of the West Indies. If they joined with us they could supply us with

products that, because of climatic conditions, we cannot produce ourselves. In turn we could supply them with many goods they are unable to produce.
Obviously there will be problems ahead. At the moment we cannot even get along with the province of Quebec on two simple problems, one being the language problem, and the other the much more important one, that the province of Quebec has never really grown up and played its role in confederation. It is like an adolescent child which has reached the stage that it is able to go out and make a few bucks, and so says, "To heck with the family that raised me. I won't contribute to the pot. I want all this for myself." Obviously Quebec is not interested in becoming a "have" province within confederation, yet for a long time as a "have not" province it has been assisted greatly in a number of fields. This is a problem that we have not been able to solve.
In the circumstances we will not be able to take on the problem of the Caribbean for quite some time. Until we are able to solve the first problem we will not be able to solve the second. In Canada we have been Simon pure so far as racial problems are concerned, simply because they have not arisen. When there are only a very few people involved it is easy to say, "There will be no discrimination." All of us have known a few people of other races in various communities, and when they are few in number it is very easy to say of one of them, "Yes, I know Joe, and he is a pretty good guy". We can look at him as an individual and not as a representative of a class of people.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
We have not had a problem similar to the Puerto Rican problem of New York, the Harlem problem or the ghetto problem of Detroit, but I believe Great Britain now is experiencing some of these problems and has not been able to solve them. This is something which must be considered if we are to extend full partnership to these islands, because this would mean that there would be an exchange of persons from the West Indies on a permanent basis who may be of a race and colour different from that of the majority of the general Canadian public. This is not an insurmountable problem; but we must reach a fairly high degree of sophistication before this partnership can take place, particularly with the political ramifications which to-date we do not seem to have been able to handle.
February 5, 1968

I believe the stature of Canada among the nations of the commonwealth would increase vastly if the government should accept this motion or give some study immediately to the feasibility of a very limited union of an economic nature. The government should consider the future implications of an economic and political union leading eventually to provincial status for the West Indies. I of course have not been to these areas. I have not spoken to many people from the smaller islands who might be interested in the type of proposal we are suggesting. However, since the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association has moved to bring a number of these delegates to Canada this year, I think the government would be well advised to consider discussing with them the possibility of at least this limited co-operation in an economic sense, and the feasibility of discussing political and provincial status arrangements.
In closing I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) for having raised this matter. I find it disconcerting that this type of motion should come from those of a conservative bent, when obviously it is something which is very progressive in outlook. I therefore doubly congratulate him. I am aware of the fact that the people in the maritime provinces have been much more interested in the expansion of Canada and have in many ways made a greater contribution to the stature of the discussions which take place in respect of the development of our nation, than those in other parts of Canada, including my province, who have always been more interested in what they can get out of the association than what they put in.
I hope arrangements will be made immediately for the expansion of export aid, and that this will be done in a meaningful way so that the people who receive it will be aware of the friendliness of the Canadian public behind the gesture. Those people in turn will be able to bring to the attention of the Canadian public, through their acceptance of the aid, the fact that this type of aid is mutual. While we may be in the position of supplying the dollars now, the benefits of the dollars in helping other countries to develop will bring greater rewards to the Canadian public as the years go by, through trade and co-operation in the commonwealth arrangement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the motion of the hon.
Trade with Caribbean Federation member for Queens. Last year and in previous years the hon. member has had a motion of a similar nature promoting closer relations with the West Indies. Last year I seized the occasion to discuss the Patrick proposal for a better Canada-West Indies relationship. Since that time some of the islands have reached independence and the Canada-West Indies conference has taken place in Ottawa.
Barbados, Trinidad and Jamaica now are full fledged independent commonwealth nations. Antigua, Dominica, St. Lucia, Grenada and others are independent states in association with Great Britain. However, as the hon. member for Queens pointed out, the constitution of these associated states permits the islands to change from a free state in association with Great Britain to a free state in association with another commonwealth country. This could be done by a very simple procedure. Some of the other islands such as Montserrat and St. Vincent are still possessions of Great Britain, having an administrator who is appointed, not elected.
As a result of last year's conference Canadian external aid to this area of the world has been greatly increased. The Canadian government will spend a minimum of $65 million in the next five years. There will be special assistance to the local university, aid in radio communications and aid in airport extension. The premiers and leaders of the islands consult and co-operate in the promotion of these projects.
The proposal for a new Canada-West Indies relationship deals mainly with the so-called little eight islands of Barbados, Antigua, St. Kitts, Montserrat, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and Grenada with a total population of about 700,000. Under the proposal Canada would assume the role of senior partner and would invite the islands to join us in a monetary and customs union. Canada would provide for their defence and external affairs representation.

Earlier I pointed out that financial interests acquire sporting organizations such as hockey, football, baseball and basketball teams, because of the cost of obtaining rights to cover programs on television and radio stations, if they have such stations under their control. Many people may think that this is unbelievable, but it is the fact. Many of these teams we follow through our newspapers, radio and television stations, are owned outright by radio and television personalities, for the reason I have mentioned.
As I have said before, this act is the greatest radio and television act one could imagine for the benefit of investors in radio and television, and if it is accepted it will have the greatest effect on sporting activities the world has ever seen. Teams are being bought up by these organizations. I should not like the public to think that for the rest of time we are going to be able to sit in our living rooms anywhere in North America and watch first class hockey games and first class world series ball games without having to pay. Many people can get hot and bothered about a C.B.C. installation forming a network to put these games into the homes of people throughout the country, but it is ridiculous to think we can force the people who have money to make all these big professional sports events available through an open

We cannot continue for ever and a day to broadcast over the open airwaves the work of professional athletes such as the hockey players, football players and baseball players without compensating them for the entertainment they bring into the homes of the nation. It is all right for people to scream that these athletes are making more money now than they ever made before, because of television, but we must remember that the participants in those leagues below the top are still being paid peanuts. We all know of the Dallas player who was suspended for seven weeks because he looked cross-eyed at a coach. Mr. Chairman, this clause and the one following it have created apparently a good deal of misunderstanding in connection with the financial provisions of the C.B.C. Since the two clauses are interrelated perhaps I might deal with them together; if not, I will deal with each individually.
The provision in the second of the two clauses is one for a five year operating budget for the C.B.C., but contrary to what seems to be the popular belief that would not in any way commit parliament to providing the C.B.C. with a five year grant.
It should not be forgotten that every single investigating body has recommended the essential importance of providing the C.B.C. with long term operational financing. That was the view that was also supported by the standing committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts after it considered the white paper in which the government had said it proposed five year financing. It was and it still remains the intention of the government to submit a special financing bill to parliament, and that would be based on a formula. The formula has yet to be worked out.
Perhaps I should say something about the kind of formula that is contemplated. The Fowler committee recommended that the number of television households in Canada should be used as an index-so many dollars per household with television. It has also been suggested that it might be in the nature of a per capita grant based on total Canadian population.
The financing legislation, according to whichever formula it adopts, would stipulate that the operating requirements of the C.B.C. would have to be met by payments from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of so much per

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting capita or per television household, or whatever the formula was. That amount would have to be paid out year by year in each of the fiscal years covered by the special financing act.
Unless and until that kind of special act is passed by this house and the other place, the C.B.C. will continue to have its operating requirements met on an annual basis through the normal estimates and appropriations procedures, even notwithstanding that clauses 46 and 47, as printed in this bill, were to pass.
With respect to capital budgets, clause 46 (1) provides that the corporation is a proprietary corporation within the meaning and for the purposes of the Financial Administration Act. Under that act all proprietary corporations are required to submit an annual capital budget, and the C.B.C., no less than others, would have to meet this requirement.
Clause 47 (1) would not nullify this requirement, since it refers only to a capital program and not to a capital budget. It is virtually identical, in effect, with section 35 (2) of the 1958 act. Its purpose, now as before, is to provide a framework for assessing the probable effects of capital expansion on the operating requirements of the corporation, and it is in no sense to be regarded as providing for a five year capital budget.
Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, both in the committee and outside the chamber several hon. members have expressed very strong opposition to the idea of long term financing for the C.B.C., and it seems to me that there is very little advantage, after the length of time we have now spent discussing the various provisions of this bill, to waste further time arguing about a clause which does not make any real provision for payment of money to the C.B.C. It is already clear that the C.B.C will have to be financed in the customary way for the fiscal year 1968-69, because they are so far along in their financing, and there will be an opportunity for discussion after the estimates have been presented.
Next session the government will bring forward a C.B.C. financing bill. This will be after the new management has had an opportunity to review the plans of the corporation. Parliament will then have an opportunity to give full consideration to whether or not long term financing would indeed be in the public interest. I want to make it quite clear that it is still the government's intention to propose long term financing, not for this year but for the period thereafter.

We should facilitate the progress of this debate if clauses 46 and 47 were to be dealt with separately. If that were done it would be necessary to delete clause 46(1), and I can explain why that is. Clause 46(1) says that the corporation is a proprietary corporation within the meaning and for the purpose of the Financial Administration Act. A proprietary corporation generally has an assured source of income. It has to submit an annual capital budget but does not have to submit an annual operating budget, since its expenditures are met from its assured revenues.
If long term financing were approved for the C.B.C., the corporation would have an assured statutory income; but until parliament has approved a long term formula for operational requirements, it is clearly necessary for the corporation to continue to submit an annual operating budget. Deleting clause 46(1) would enable us to treat the C.B.C. as an agency of the corporation until parliament has approved long term financing; and agency corporations are required, under the Financial Administration Act, to submit an annual capital budget and an annual operating budget.

Mention it when you go out west.

I was given by the department a copy of a picture which they said was a farm wagon manufactured by a particular company. If this amendment is to protect that type of transaction, I am opposed to it. In other words, in my opinion this clause is discriminatory. I suggest that the minister would be quite in order in allowing us to add the two words "and trucks" to the clause. In so far as a bilateral agreement with West Germany is concerned, there is a real legal
DEBATES	February 5, 1968
difficulty involved since Canada has no standing in international law to represent these persons with respect to claims which arose before they became Canadians. Furthermore, the Bonn Agreements of 1952, and the fact that no peace treaty has ever been signed with Germany, also present difficulties.
I am convinced that in these circumstances the government can be of most assistance to these persons by making informal approaches to the German authorities and using our good office where appropriate in individual cases. This is the policy which has long been followed by this department. Our embassy in Bonn has had discussions on this matter with the German authorities on a number of occasions. The German authorities are fully aware of the desire of the Canadian government that they take as forthright an attitude as possible on the question of indemnification.
Moreover, our representative on the executive committee of the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has spoken on this question a number of times. It should be noted, however, that West Germany has endeavoured to meet its responsibilities. The relevant West German legislation was liberalized in 1965 and a second fund was established with the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in 1967 for the benefit of persons who had not been indemnified along the lines advocated by Canada and other interested nations. We shall of course continue to pursue with the West German authorities the possibility of any further measures which may be feasible.
I should like to assure the house that the Canadian government takes this question very seriously and makes every effort to assist these unfortunate persons who have suffered through no fault of their own from the acts of the nazi regime. maintopic: EDUCATION-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE IN TEACHING IMMIGRANT CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to reconsider the government's refusal to share in meeting the extra expenses involved in giving special English classes to immigrant children. I took advantage of the rules to raise this matter again, as it is of great importance. The problem to which I drew attention has become acute in Toronto where, according to the chairman of the board of education, out of
29.000	immigrant children who need help only
11.000	are getting it. But it is a serious one in


all major Canadian cities; I mention specifically the city of Montreal. It is my opinion that the government has been shirking its responsibilities in this field and sheltering beneath the umbrella of a false constitutional issue.
What are the facts? The Canadian government is responsible for immigration. It brings to this country thousands of skilled and other immigrants and in order to persuade these immigrants to come here, as well as on grounds of humanity and family considerations, it necessarily brings the children of those immigrants, most of whom go to our major cities. In the white paper on immigration in 1966 the government admitted responsibility for immigrants after they come to Canada, in the following words:
People who come to Canada should receive the kind of services they need to start productive employment as soon as possible. They may need language training.
A little later we find this:
Sufficient financial and personal resources will be made available to ensure that no immigrant may lack any help he may want in getting established.
As a matter of fact, the department of immigration does assist in providing English classes for adult immigrants. But when it comes to classes for children, the answer of the government is, no. In other words, children with special problems in acquiring sufficient English to fit successfully into our normal school system are perhaps being kept out of future productive employment or even handicapped for life.
What is the excuse? The excuse is that education is a provincial subject and that therefore the federal government cannot touch it. I agree that education is a provincial subject, but in the light of its responsibility toward immigrants it is perfectly proper and possible for the government to meet the special needs of immigrants before they move into the main stream of education.
I challenge the minister, or whoever is to reply, to tell us that Indian children and the children of servicemen serving overseas are not supported by the federal government, notwithstanding the so-called constitutional barrier. I assert that the only bar to helping these children is an imaginary and false constitutional difficulty. These children are in effect wards of the federal government. They have been invited to Canada and permitted to enter in conformity with federal policy. I call on the minister in the name of common sense, in the name of the basic immigration policies
February 5, 1968
COMMONS DEBATES	6403
of this government and in the name of basic fairness to those concerned, to reconsider his policy in respect to these immigrant children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, throughout the years, to my knowledge during the last 15 years at least, members on all sides of the house have received representations and letters from the representatives of various national groups in Canada who prior to coming to this country suffered in nazi concentration camps. I have a great deal of sympathy for these people because of what they have suffered. I think they are in a similar category to all other persons who suffered in these camps.
I have heard from them in Winnipeg, Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. Quite recently I received another letter signed by the chairman and the secretary general of the Polish Political Ex-Prisoners Association in Canada, Inc., of 1087 Queen street west, Toronto 3, and it puts the question forward with more
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion logic and sequence than I could manage in seven minutes. It reads:
Dear Member:
Twenty-two years have passed since the survivors of Nazi concentration camps were set free by the Allied armies. Many of them, due to the fact that their homelands were ruled by communist dictatorship, remained in western Europe, and eventually found their way to Canada, where they have established new homes, acquired Canadian citizenship and contribute to the development of this country.
The injury inflicted on many of them, however, has never been made good. The work of the Canadian War Commission, which concluded its activities before the bulk of the new Canadians arrived, has not benefited them at all. The German authorities, while in principle professing that every injury would be compensated, have only provided compensation for persons persecuted because of race or religion, while those persecuted for reason of nationality were promised only greatly reduced benefits, provided they were refugees on October 1st 1953 and provided that they suffered at least a 25 per cent disability. In practice one per cent of the claimants in this category has been in receipt of their meagre pensions so far.
For over 15 years the Canadian-Polish organizations and individuals have made representations to the successive Canadian administrations, bringing to the government's attention the plight of persons in positions who, due to hardship suffered and disabilities acquired during their incarceration are already, or likely to become, charges of the Canadian welfare organizations and a substantial burden to the taxpayer. It is only reasonable to expect that the country which perpetrated the atrocities and crimes ought to compensate the victims. As we have indicated, the results have been far from satisfactory.
In March 1965, a brief was submitted to the Prime Minister through the Hon. Paul Martin, Minister for External Affairs, by the delegation of the Polish Political Ex-Prisoners Inc., which represents over 1,300 persons (of 15 different nationalities, but the majority of which are of Polish origin) asking the government to take steps toward the conclusion of a bilateral agreement with Germany, and to obtain a lump sum payment in settlement of the claims by Canadian citizens or residents, who have not at all, or inadequately, been compensated by the German authorities.
The letter concludes:
As Canadian citizens we former prisoners of Nazi death camps are, in theory, entitled to all the privileges of a born Canadian, but in practice we are deprived of the protection of the Canadian government. As people who have fought and suffered for the Allied cause longer and more extensively than any others, we take the liberty of soliciting your support for our just claims.
The association demands that the administration:-
(1)	Either concludes a bilateral agreement with the Federal Republic of Germany for the compensation for all Canadian citizens and residents who have suffered persecution but have not been properly compensated or-
(2)	Enacts legislation establishing a special Canadian agency to deal with such persons and award
6404	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion them pensions, retroactive to 1945, or enable Veterans Affairs ministry to award such pensions.
It is hoped that with your kind understanding and co-operation, our just cause may find a solution in the near future.
It was on that account that on February 1 I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I must say that in his brief absence he has been missed by us all. Has the government received representations from any organization representing Canadian citizens who are survivors of nazi concentration camps urging that a bilateral agreement be made with the federal government of Germany for the compensation of all Canadian citizens and residents who have suffered persecution but have not been properly compensated to date?
At that point, Mr. Speaker, you cut me down again as on previous occasions. However, I should like the parliamentary secretary when he replies to inform us what the government has done to date, and what it intends to do.
